The last item alone runs 74 words. On a phone this is roughly a full screen of unbroken text introducing four unfamiliar named concepts before the reader gets a single example to hold on to. content/questions/testing.json solves this exact shape with a bulleted list; tdd.json never does.

worst_places.after:
A few concrete, recognizable smells show up again and again in large suites.

- **Assertion Roulette** — a test with many unlabelled assertions. When it fails, you cannot tell which assertion broke without adding print statements or stepping through a debugger. *Fix:* split it into focused, single-purpose tests, or give every assertion a descriptive failure message.
- **Mystery Guest** — a test that depends on state defined far away from the test itself: a shared fixture file, a seeded database row. A reader cannot tell what is being set up just by reading the test. *Fix:* make the setup explicit and local to the test, even if that means repeating a few lines.

The goal here is just correctness, not design.

worst_places.after:
TDD (Test-Driven Development) works in three short phases that repeat.

**Red.** You write a test for behaviour that doesn't exist yet, and you run it. It must fail, because there is no implementation. This forces you to decide the API and the expected result before writing any code.

**Green.** You write the smallest amount of code that makes the test pass, even if it is ugly. The goal is correctness only, not design.

**Refactor.** Now you have a passing test as a safety net, so you clean the implementation up: better names, no duplication, simpler logic. The behaviour stays the same. If you break something, the test suite says so immediately.

```
Red  ──►  Green  ──►  Refactor
 ▲                        │
 └────────────────────────┘
```

worst_places.quote: The choice depends on what the test actually needs to prove: use a stub when you just need the dependency to return something so the rest of the logic can run; use a mock when the *fact that a call happened* is the behavior you're testing (e.g., "an email was sent"); use a spy when you want the real logic to execute but still need to confirm a specific call happened; use a fake when a stub would be too simplistic and a full real dependency is too slow or unavailable in tests.

worst_places.before: The choice depends on what the test actually needs to prove: use a stub when you just need the dependency to return something so the rest of the logic can run; use a mock when the *fact that a call happened* is the behavior you're testing (e.g., "an email was sent"); use a spy when you want the real logic to execute but still need to confirm a specific call happened; use a fake when a stub would be too simplistic and a full real dependency is too slow or unavailable in tests.
worst_places.after:
Pick the one that matches what the test needs to prove:

- **Stub** — you just need the dependency to return something, so the rest of the logic can run.
- **Mock** — the *fact that a call happened* is the behaviour under test ("an email was sent").
- **Spy** — you want the real logic to run, but you also need to confirm a specific call happened.
- **Fake** — a stub would be too simplistic, and the real dependency is too slow or not available in tests.

worst_places.after: Real timers make this kind of test both slow and flaky. A retry-with-backoff test that uses real `setTimeout` delays burns real seconds on every run. And CI machines (the shared build servers that run your tests) are usually slower and busier than your laptop. So a delay that is only just long enough locally will sometimes run out of time on CI, and the test fails for no real reason.

patterns: The dominant structural habit: where content/questions/testing.json introduces N parallel concepts as a bulleted list, tdd.json runs them together inside one paragraph with bolded run-in labels. Red / Green / Refactor (q-1), the four qualities of a good unit test (q-2), the three AAA steps (q-4), the three pyramid levels (q-5), the four test doubles (q-9), the three layers of an API endpoint (q-14), the four test smells (q-23), the three parts of the flaky-test strategy (q-25). This one habit produces nearly all 40+ over-long paragraphs the script flags and every wall of theory in the file. Converting these to lists — no wording changes at all — would fix most of B and D at once.

Every mid-level and senior answer contains one 'decision rule' sentence delivered as a single 60-96-word chain of semicolon-separated branches: q-7 ('the decision comes down to three questions...'), q-9 ('the choice depends on what the test actually needs to prove...'), q-18 (the two-axis risk framework), q-19 (the incremental-CI approach), q-22 ('the practical, senior-level resolution...'). These are the most valuable sentences in the bank and the least readable ones; each is a table pretending to be prose.

The bank argues from named authorities and named patterns without ever introducing them: TDD itself, BDD, DHH, Uncle Bob, Michael Feathers, London/Detroit/Chicago schools, AST, DI. Well-known-inside-the-community names are treated as public knowledge, while genuinely obscure pattern names that the author chose to teach (seam, characterization test, Assertion Roulette, Mystery Guest, equivalent mutants) are all carefully defined. The file knows how to explain a term; it just does not notice which ones need it.

Typographically the file is a straight import of an English source: 162 spaced hyphens and zero em-dashes in the RU locale, against 150 em-dashes in content/questions/testing.json#ru. In Russian a spaced hyphen does not signal a clause break, so on a phone every parenthetical aside has to be re-parsed. Four RU headings are also left fully in English.
notes:
Overlap verdict: keep two banks, but stop re-teaching. 8 of 26 tdd entries cover the same ground as testing.json: pyramid (tdd-q-5 vs testing-q-1/q-16), test doubles (tdd-q-9 vs testing-q-6), snapshot (tdd-q-13 vs testing-q-9), mutation testing (tdd-q-19 vs testing-q-22), contract testing (tdd-q-20 vs testing-q-17), property-based (tdd-q-21 vs testing-q-18), micro-frontends (tdd-q-26 vs testing-q-21), shared-state/order dependence (tdd-q-23 vs testing-q-14). The two question banks never contradict each other — they agree everywhere and simply repeat, and tdd's versions of mutation testing and property-based testing are the deeper ones while testing's version of contract testing is. All actual contradictions in the topic live in content/quiz/testing.json (see the sibling report).
Recommendation: split by intent — tdd.json = process, design pressure, legacy adoption, pragmatism; testing.json = tools and techniques. For the four senior duplicates, keep whichever version is deeper and have the other cross-reference it. tdd-q-5 in particular is a near-verbatim second telling of testing-q-1, including the same three-example code shape, and is the clearest candidate for removal or reduction to a pointer.
Because neither `testing` nor `tdd` has a theory article, this bank is the site's only explanation of red-green-refactor, AAA and the test-double taxonomy — which is why the missing TDD expansion, the run-in walls in the junior entries (q-1 to q-5) and the total absence of any diagram are scored harder than they would be in a bank that sits behind an article.
